claims.claim: Encoding is the process of turning experience into a memory trace — the first stage of the memory sequence. The APA Dictionary of Psychology defines encoding as the conversion of a sensory input into a form capable of being processed and deposited in memory, the first stage followed by retention and then retrieval; OpenStax Psychology 2e describes encoding as the input of information into the memory system; the Noba Project describes encoding as transforming a physical, sensory input into a representation that can be stored.

Psychologists distinguish three main types of encoding by the kind of information used: acoustic encoding (by sound), visual encoding (by image), and semantic encoding (by meaning). The APA Dictionary of Psychology has a separate entry for each type, and OpenStax Psychology 2e describes all three as ways information gets into memory.

The depth-of-processing account (Craik and Lockhart, 1972, as reported by OpenStax Psychology 2e and the Noba Project) holds that how deeply information is processed determines how well it is remembered: shallow processing works on surface features such as sound, while deep processing works on meaning and produces more durable memories — meaning beats repetition.

Encoding requires attention: the APA Dictionary of Psychology defines attention as the process of focusing on selected aspects of the environment while ignoring others, and OpenStax Psychology 2e states that information must be attended to in order to be encoded well enough to remember.

Encoding strategies help information get in: chunking organizes material into meaningful groups (APA Dictionary; OpenStax 8.4), mnemonics are memory aids that give information structure (APA Dictionary; OpenStax 8.4), and rehearsal comes in two forms — maintenance rehearsal (repetition that holds information in short-term memory) and elaborative rehearsal (linking new material to existing knowledge, which supports longer-lasting encoding) — both defined by the APA Dictionary and recommended by OpenStax 8.4.

The honest note: encoding strategies help, but none guarantees a memory. OpenStax Psychology 2e 8.4 recommends the strategies as ways to enhance memory, while the Noba Project describes remembering as reconstructive and fallible — a trace can fade and retrieval can fail even for well-encoded material, so strategies improve odds rather than seal deals.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The depth-of-processing account is a framework, not a precise theory: it has been criticized for not specifying what 'depth' means independently of the memory outcomes it predicts.
positions: Craik and Lockhart (1972): deeper processing of meaning produces more durable memories (OpenStax, Noba).
Critics note that 'depth' is hard to define without reference to the remembering it is meant to explain.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents depth of processing with attribution as an account that explains why meaning-based study tends to outperform repetition, without treating it as an exact law.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Encoding strategies are recommended as effective, yet no strategy guarantees memory.
positions: OpenStax 8.4 presents chunking, mnemonics, and rehearsal as effective ways to enhance memory.
The same sources describe memory as reconstructive and fallible (Noba), so strategy effectiveness is a matter of improving the odds.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the strategies as helpful and includes an explicit honest note that they do not guarantee memory, consistent with both positions.
